nodes.text: SERMONS OF ST FULGENTIUS.
FIRST SERMON.
On the Stewards of the Lord.

1. The Lord's word, which we all ought to hear not only eagerly but also wisely, and which we must obey humbly and with delight, keeps everywhere the balance of its moderation, so that neither do the sheep lack pasture nor the shepherds food; some things it commands specially to us alone, but some generally both to us and to you. For to us, that is, to the servants whom that father of the household, the Lord of all things, has set in his great house for this purpose, that we may minister the word of grace to his people, the office of holy preaching is specially enjoined; but generally, to us and to you, saving obedience to the commandments is prescribed. In these commandments, again, as in the richest dishes, the spiritual abundance of heavenly delights so overflows that in the word of God there is plenty for the mature to eat, and plenty also for the little one to suck. For there is at once both the drink of milk, by which the tender infancy of the faithful is nourished, and solid food, by which the robust youth of the mature receives the spiritual growth of holy virtue. There, in short, provision is made for the salvation of all whom the Lord deigns to save; there is what suits every age, there what befits every calling; there we hear the precepts we are to do, there we learn the rewards we are to hope for; there is the command which teaches us through the letter and instructs us to knowledge; there the promise which through grace draws and leads us to glory.

2. The Lord, then, wishing to show the special office of the servants whom he has set over his people, says, as we have just heard from the Gospel: Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward, whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due time? Blessed is that servant whom the Lord, when he comes, finds so doing (Luke 12:42–43). Who is this Lord, brothers? Christ without doubt, who says to his disciples: You call me Master and Lord; and you say well, for so I am (John 13:13). And what is the household of this Lord? Surely it is the one which the Lord himself redeemed from the hand of the enemy and made over to his own ownership. This household is the holy Catholic Church, which spreads through the world with abundant fruitfulness and glories that it has been redeemed by the precious blood of its Lord. For the Son of Man, as he himself says, came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Matt. 20:28). He is also the Good Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep. So the flock of the Good Shepherd is the very household of the Redeemer. But who the steward is, who must be both faithful and prudent, the apostle Paul shows us, speaking of himself and his companions: Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here, moreover, it is required among stewards that one be found faithful (1 Cor. 4:1–2).

3. But lest any of us think that only the apostles were made stewards, and, neglecting the duty of spiritual warfare, sleep as a lazy servant, unfaithfully and imprudently, the blessed Apostle himself, showing that bishops too are stewards, says: For a bishop must be blameless, as God's steward (Titus 1:7). We are, then, servants of the father of the household, we are stewards of the Lord, we have received the measure of wheat to pay out to you. And if we ask what this measure of wheat is, the blessed apostle Paul shows us this too, saying: To each as God has apportioned the measure of faith (Rom. 12:3). So what Christ names the measure of wheat, Paul calls the measure of faith, so that we may recognise that the spiritual wheat is nothing other than the venerable sacrament of the Christian faith. We give you the measure of this wheat in the name of the Lord whenever, enlightened by the gift of spiritual grace, we discourse according to the rule of the true faith; and you receive that same measure of wheat through the Lord's stewards when daily you hear the word of truth through the servants of God. Let us now, then, speak of this very measure of wheat. From it, as God has apportioned, let us all be fed; from it let us take the nourishment of a good life, so that we may be able to attain the rewards of eternal life, believing in him, hoping in him, loving him above all and in all, who gives himself to us both as nourishment, so that we do not faint on the way, and keeps himself as reward, so that we may rejoice in the homeland. For Christ is our nourishment, Christ will be our reward; Christ is the food and comfort of travellers on the road, he himself the fullness and exultation of the blessed at rest. To this measure of wheat, therefore, belongs what the Lord says: Sell what you possess, and give alms; make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, a treasure that does not fail in the heavens, where no thief comes near and no moth corrupts (Luke 12:33). It is a great good, dearest brothers, very fitting, very profitable, and above all to be sought by all Christians, that none should take pleasure in falling away to worse, but that all of us should strive to advance to better.

4. We are trees, brothers, planted in the Lord's field. And God is our husbandman: he rains upon us, he tends us, he himself gives fruitfulness, he himself supplies the grace of bearing fruit. The rain of God is the word of holy preaching; the tending of God is the infusion of spiritual grace. God, then, rains upon us by his precept and tends us by his help. When he rains, he takes from us the dryness of ignorance; when he tends, he grants the richness of living well; when he rains, he waters the soil of our heart; and when he tends, he roots out of that soil the thorns and thistles of worldly desire. We ought therefore to be made fruitful by the heavenly rains; we ought to answer the hands of the heavenly husbandman with fitting fruit. And if not all trees can bear equal fruit, yet none ought to remain barren in the Lord's field.

5. Greatly to be feared by us, brothers, is that sentence of the one who threatens, in which it is said: Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matt. 3:10). If barrenness is thrown into the fire, what does rapacity deserve? Or what will he receive who has taken what belongs to another, if he who has not given of his own will burn for ever? And if judgement will be without mercy for him who has not shown mercy (James 2:13), what kind of judgement will there be for him who has committed robbery as well? Let us fear, then, brothers, let us fear our deeds. Let him who obeys Christ sell what he possesses and give alms, so that he may lift his heart from earth to heaven, trample on avarice, hasten with the whole intent of his mind to the summit of perfection, and be anxious not about the things of the world but about the things of the Lord; so that he may have the world crucified to him and show himself crucified to the world; so that he may be wholly poor in this age and rich in Christ. Who does not know the greatness of this good?

6. But we see that not all have the strength to sell their possessions. For each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that (1 Cor. 7:7). See, this so great good few can fulfil, many cannot. Because this perfection is given to few, must all those who cannot yet be perfect in good therefore be utterly wicked? Must a Christian therefore persist in the vice of rapacity because perhaps he cannot yet pay out all his goods to the poor? Or must he covet what belongs to others because he cannot yet wholly despise what is his own? Far be this, brothers, from all Christians; may God turn this away from his faithful. For the Apostle truly says that neither the avaricious nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6:10). And it is plain that all who will be estranged from the kingdom of God will be condemned in eternal fire with the devil and his angels.

7. Therefore, dearest ones, if not all can fulfil what the Lord says, Sell what you possess (Luke 12:33), yet what he added, saying, Give alms (ibid.), is possible for all, if good will is present; easy for all, if dire greed is absent; wholesome for all, if charity is fervent: so it ought to be common to all, so that eternal happiness may be given to all. He, then, who receives from the Lord such strength that for love of the heavenly kingdom he despises everything in the world, let him sell what he has and spend it on the needy. But he who is not yet of such strength, let him give alms from what he has, as far as he has. Let good will do as much as means allow. Let the perfect hold the first place of virtue; let the imperfect at least reach the second. Let the one become gloriously worthy; let the other be praiseworthily generous. Let the one be the most ardent lover of holy poverty; let the other be the most devoted comforter of the holy poor. Let the latter have as patrons before God the poor, whom the former rejoices to have as companions in virtue. Let the one be such as to sit with the Lord to judge; let the other be such as to stand at the right hand to be judged. Let the one be such as to possess the eternal dwellings by perpetual right; let the other be such that the former receives him. For the Lord admonishes us, saying: Make for yourselves friends of the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9).

8. This, then, brothers, is necessary for all of us: that no one be sluggish in good works, no one be barren, no one through love of present things despise the things to come, no one, despising the eternal, perversely look only at the temporal; no one prefer bodily things to spiritual, no one put earthly things before heavenly. Let us place our treasure in heaven, brothers, so that we may also have our heart in heaven. For it must be that where the treasure of our love has gone ahead, there the affection of our thought also follows. Therefore the Truth says: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also (Matt. 6:21). So, that we may lay up treasure in heaven, let us love heavenly things. Do you want to know where you are laying up treasure? Look at what you love. Do you want to know what you love? Look at what you think about. So it will come about that you recognise your treasure from your love, and understand your love from the evidence of your thought. And the Lord, showing how we can lay up treasure in heaven, says: Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning (Luke 12:35).

9. If we wish to take this saying of the Lord according to the letter, [we can find] nothing of spiritual benefit in it [...] in the [girded loins] and burning lamps a spiritual understanding must be sought, one that is worthy of the divine precept and is found fitting and beneficial for our salvation. For not in vain does the Lord himself say in a certain place: The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life (John 6:63). So in the loins fleshly desire is shown, while in the lamps Christian faith and charity are displayed. Therefore when the Lord orders our loins to be girded, he undoubtedly commands that the desires of the flesh be curbed. And when he commands that we have burning lamps, he certainly orders this: that we both shine with the light of true faith and glow with the works of holy charity. In ordering that our loins be girded, he commands that we flee evil desires and deeds; in ordering that our lamps be burning, he admonishes us to love and do what is good.

10. Let us compare these words that we have put forward from the Gospel with the words of the prophets. For one God established both Testaments, one Lord gave [them]; and though the sacraments of the two Testaments differ according to the times, yet in both the teaching on human salvation agrees, by which we are commanded not to sin, and ordered to persevere in good works. So the Lord commands through blessed David, saying: Turn away from evil, and do good (Ps. 33:15). Through Isaiah too he admonishes all with these words: Take away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes; cease to act perversely, learn to do well (Isa. 1:16). What the Lord now commands in his own person, then, he also enjoined on us through the holy patriarchs and prophets. For what is Let your loins be girded, but Turn away from evil? What is Let the lamps be burning, but Do good? What is Let your loins be girded, but Cease to act perversely? What is Let the lamps be burning, but Learn to do well?

11. The loins of the faithful, then, are girded when evil desire is suppressed, when wicked thought is restrained, when the mind resists lust, when affection is denied to wantonness, when luxury is trampled down, when avarice and robbery are despised, when harm to one's neighbour is avoided, when pride is conquered, when envy is overcome. And the lamps of the faithful burn when they keep the rule of right faith, when they persevere patiently in the bosom of mother Church, when they despise earthly things and long for heavenly ones, when they carefully guard peace, when they love one another purely, when they outdo one another in showing honour, when they advance in meekness and humility of heart, when they do works of mercy willingly and cheerfully, and when in good works they strive to please not men but God.

12. So let every Christian have his loins girded, that he may flee lust; let him have a burning lamp, that he may guard chastity. Let him have his loins girded, that he may neither seize nor steal anything belonging to another; let him have a burning lamp, that he may work mercifully from what is his own. Let him have his loins girded, that he may not oppress the lesser; let him have a burning lamp, that he may give the oppressed the help of a just defence under the cover of justice. Let him have his loins girded, that he may not take food from one who has it; let him have a burning lamp, that he may give nourishment to the hungry. Let him have his loins girded, that he may not strip the clothed; let him have a burning lamp, that he may clothe the naked. Let him have his loins girded, that he may invade no one's house; let him have a burning lamp, that he may willingly receive the strangers of Christ. Let him have his loins girded, that he may flee haughtiness; let him have a burning lamp, that he may keep humility. Let him have his loins girded, that he may drive envy and spite from himself; let him have a burning lamp, that he may show pure charity to all. Let him have his loins girded, that he may not offer his members as weapons of iniquity to sin; let him have a burning lamp, that he may offer his members as weapons of justice to God (Rom. 6:13).

13. This, brothers, is the true and sound teaching of the catholic faith. This is the measure of wheat with which the household of the Lord the Redeemer is to be fed. From this we give to you, as much as the Lord grants; and we continually entreat the Lord himself that he may deign by his help to feed both us and you in the fear of his grace. May he take from us the dominion of depraved desire, and give to all progress and perseverance in charity. May he himself gird our loins, may he himself make our lamps burn and keep them burning, so that neither our charity grows cold nor any iniquity rules over us. But may our Lord and Redeemer grant grace to all, and pour into all the gift of holy illumination and strength. May he grant us to understand rightly what we hear from him and to do it as we ought, and to preach to you what is to be done in sufficient and fitting words. May he grant you too both to understand in your heart and to do in deed what you hear from him through his servants. May the divine mercy, then, work this in all of us, that [he] may have us, whom he willed to be stewards, as useful ones.
SERMON II.
On the twofold Nativity of Christ, the one eternal from the Father, the other temporal from the Virgin.

1. Wishing to say something about the solemnity of this day, and at the same time considering that one Word of which we wish to speak, we find no words with which we can say anything adequately. For this Word is not one that ceases once uttered, but one that remains, being born; not transitory, but eternal; not made by God the Father, but begotten; and not only begotten, but Only-begotten. For God the Father begot one Word from himself, through whom he created all things out of nothing. For in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3). And in this, that God the Father made all things through that Word, it is shown that he begot this Word, and did not make it. That Word, then, is God from God, creator from creator. Hence he has by nature in himself to be what the Father is.

2. So God the Son was born of God the Father, another in person, not other in nature: always with the Father, always together with the Father, always from the Father, always in the Father; always with the Father, with whom he has one natural immensity; always together with the Father, with whom he has one natural eternity; always from the Father, from whom he has by nature an eternal birth; always in the Father, with whom he has by nature one and equal divinity. And the one who is the Father is indeed one, and the one who is the Son is another; yet neither is another God, because the Father and the Son are one God. Therefore, when discourse arises concerning God the Father and God the Son, we rightly say that the Father is one and the Son another; and nonetheless we rightly say that the Father and the Son are one God. For when we say that the Father is one and the Son another, we point out the distinct persons of begetter and begotten; but when we say that the Father and the Son are one God, we show the one nature itself of undivided divinity. For the person of the begetter and of the begotten is distinct, but the nature of the begetter and of the begotten is one.

3. But how will anyone be able to speak adequately or worthily? About whom? Man about God, mortal about immortal, visible about invisible, changeable about unchangeable, the work about the workman, the creature about the creator, the thing made about the maker, the little one about the immeasurable, the temporal about the eternal, the lowly about the most high, one formed from clay about him who created all things out of nothing. His is the unutterable [...] he made freely [the work] of omnipotence, and omnipotently fulfilled the work of saving grace: there having the power to found and govern his creation, here having the power to lay down and take up his life for us. Omnipotence we call that by which the Word, which was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God, made everything that was not; grace, that by which the Word made flesh came to seek and save what had perished; omnipotence, by which he made every day; grace, by which he deigned to be conceived on a certain day and born on a certain day.

4. The same one, then, made a little lower than the angels, was made in the day of men, who, coeternal and equal with God the Father, is always the day of the holy angels. For of him the prophet says: Announce well day from day, his salvation (Ps. 95:2). What is day from day, if not the Son from the Father? The Son, then, is from the Father, day from day; yet the Father and the Son are not two days, but are one day. The Son is from the Father, God from God; yet the Father and the Son are not two gods, but are one God. So the Father and the Son together are acknowledged by us as the one day of eternity, but in the day of time the Son alone is found. For the eternal day, the Father and the Son, made our body and soul; but in the day of time the Son alone took up our body and soul. Christ the eternal day, the Only-begotten, abiding in the form of God; Christ in the day of time, the Only-begotten, taking the form of a servant. Christ the eternal day, remaining rich so as to create us; Christ in the day of time, made poor so as to redeem us. The eternal day, Christ God from God the Father; Christ in the day of time, God [and] man from the virgin mother. Christ the eternal day, the Word uttered forth (Ps. 44:1) from the heart of the Father; Christ in the day of time, the Word made flesh from the womb of the virgin mother. Christ the eternal day, true God from true God; Christ in the day of time, the bridegroom coming forth from his chamber (Ps. 18:6). Christ the day of eternity, creating angels; Christ the day in time, saving men. Christ the day of eternity, feeding the holy angels in heaven; Christ the day of time, refreshing men on earth. For so that man might eat the bread of angels, the creator of angels became man, feeding both and remaining whole. How good is the bread that both feeds the angels by sight, so that they are filled with it in the homeland, and feeds us by faith, so that we do not faint on the way! That bread, which gives itself to the angels for the joy of steadfastness, gave itself to men for the remedy of health; and he who is the food of angels became medicine for us.

5. But here, dearly beloved brothers, consider the greatness of grace, and recognise what God deigned to bestow on man in advance. For Christ the Son of God, true God from true God, and by nature one God with the Father, always feeds the holy angels from himself; and yet the Son of God did not take on the nature of angels. But so that God might commend his love in us, his Son took our nature from us: and so that God the Only-begotten, who is the bread of angels, might make himself the bread of men also, he took up at once both the soul and the flesh of a man. He took each as true, each as holy, each as clean: he took our soul without iniquity, he took our flesh with mortality; he took a just soul, through which he might restore justice to our souls, but he deigned to have mortal flesh for this reason, that dying according to it he might conquer death, and according to it also rise again, through which he might raise up our bodies too.

6. A great mystery, dearly beloved brothers, a great sign of divine love. Man, despising God, departed from God; God, loving man, came to men. He loved the ungodly, to make him just; he loved the weak, to make him sound; he loved the perverse, to make him upright; he loved the dead, to make him alive. And what more shall I say? Since God the Only-begotten loved human nature so much that he not only freed it from the power of the evil angel, but also set it in himself above all the good angels at the right hand of the Father. For the nature which in the first man had been taken captive by the evil angel now itself reigns in the second man above all the good angels. The nature which in the first man polluted the world with sin itself in the second man cleansed the world from sin. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly (1 Cor. 15:47). A woman corrupt in mind deceived the first man; a virgin of uncorrupted virginity conceived the second man. In the wife of the first man the wickedness of the devil depraved her seduced mind, but in the mother of the second man the grace of God preserved both mind and flesh intact: it bestowed on the mind a most firm faith, it took from the flesh all lust entirely. Since, then, man was wretchedly condemned for sin, therefore God [made] man was wonderfully born without sin.

7. Consider, brothers, the lines of healing grace shown to us by divine kindness. Then the evil angel approached Eve, so that through her man, whom God had made, might be separated from God; but now the good angel came to Mary, so that in her God the Only-begotten might be united to human nature. The devil came to Eve, so that the malignant one might take life away from us; Gabriel came to Mary, to announce that life was to be restored to men. Through the guilt of the first man the devil began to lord it over man; through the grace of the second man he began to be overcome by man: proud over the first, captive under the second. Through the former he held us captive; through the latter he lost us, set free. The first Adam became for us the author of guilt; the last Adam became for us the author of grace. The former, formed from clay, brought forth earthly men; the latter, born of the Holy Spirit, made [men] heavenly. Through the former we lost the earlier grace; through the latter we received a greater one. For the former brought on us the stain of sin, with which we would be born to punishment; the latter conferred on us the grace of justification, so that we might be reborn to the kingdom. Through the former, carnal generation made us sons of the world; through the latter, spiritual generation presented us as sons of God. The former subjected us to vices; the latter made us flourish in virtues. The former cast us down through vices to where he first fell; the latter raises us through virtues to where he first ascended. For the former first fell into hell; the latter first ascended into heaven.

8. Meanwhile, brothers, it is fitting that on the day of the Lord's Nativity you should also solemnly hear of the day of the Lord's Resurrection. For God the Only-begotten, just as he deigned to be born for us, so he deigned to die for us according to the flesh, and deigned also to be raised. For this day is [the day] of visitation, that one of redemption. For the work of grace by which God the Only-begotten saved us he began when conceived in the womb; and that same work of grace he completed when raised from the tomb. Conceived in the womb, he became a sharer in our death; rising from the tomb, he made us sharers in his life. Now therefore let us all beseech the Lord that, just as on this day he gave joy to his people, so he may lead us all with joy and peace to that day also, and keep his people in faith and love. Amen.
SERMON III.
On Saint Stephen the protomartyr, and the Conversion of Saint

Paul. 1. Yesterday we celebrated the birth in time of our everlasting King; today we celebrate the triumphal passion of [his] soldier. For yesterday our King, clothed in the robe of flesh, coming forth from the hall of the virginal womb, deigned to visit the world; today the soldier, going out from the tent of the body, departed in triumph to heaven. The former, keeping the majesty of everlasting deity, taking up the servile girdle of flesh, entered the field of this world to fight; the latter, having laid aside the corruptible garments of the body, ascended to the palace of heaven to reign for ever. The former descended veiled in flesh; the latter ascended crowned with blood. The latter ascended while the Jews stoned [him], because the former descended while the angels rejoiced. Glory to God in the highest (Luke 2:14), the holy angels sang yesterday, exulting; today, rejoicing, they received Stephen into their company. Yesterday the Lord went out from the womb of the virgin; today the servant went forth from the prison-house of the flesh. Yesterday Christ was wrapped in swaddling cloths for us; today Stephen was clothed by him with the robe of immortality. Yesterday the narrowness of a manger held the infant Christ; today the immensity of heaven received Stephen in triumph. The Lord descended alone, so as to raise up many; our King humbled himself, so as to exalt his soldiers. For he who prepared the womb of a virgin for his own body himself deigned to open heaven to his martyr. The Lord Christ did not disdain to enter the narrowness of the womb, so that the breadth of heaven might receive the soul of Stephen.

2. It is necessary for us, dearest brothers, to recognise with what arms Stephen was girded so that he could overcome the savagery of the Jews, and so deserve to triumph happily. For such courage and such a triumph are not to be thought little of. Nor indeed could he have been fortified with cheap arms who could not be overcome by many. For in him shone the mark of unconquered courage, which neither feared the savagery of those raging (another reading: of the crowds) nor gave way, overcome by the blows of those stoning [him]. For he remained so undaunted (another reading: fearless) among those raging, and was so secure amid the torments of the stones, that he confidently rebuked the unbelief of the Jews, and kindly prayed for those stoning [him]. What, then, is this kind of arms, so great and insuperable, fortified with which he rebuked the raging and did not fear; did not strike back at those stoning him, but overcame them by enduring; and moreover, though slain, entered the hall of the heavenly kingdom alive and crowned? Without doubt, fenced about with royal protection, he was in no way overcome by his adversaries: for our King, though he is most high, came humble for our sake, but could not come empty-handed. For he brought a great donative to his soldiers, with which he not only enriched them abundantly but also strengthened them to fight unconquerably. For he brought the gift of love, by which to lead men into fellowship with the deity. What he brought, therefore, he paid out: nor did he diminish anything of his own, but wonderfully both enriched the poverty of his own and himself remained full of unfailing treasures.

3. Love, therefore, which brought Christ down from heaven to earth, itself raised Stephen from earth to heaven. The love which went before in the King itself shone forth afterwards in the soldier. O power of the Saviour, everywhere to be wondered at! O grace of the Redeemer, to be proclaimed unceasingly! He showed in the mother the miracle of everlasting virginity; he displayed in the martyr the sign of unconquered love. For integrity remained undefiled in the virgin; the strength of affection persevered unconquered in the martyr. And just as in the mother of the Lord virginity could not be violated, so in the martyr's mind the love of Christ could not be overcome by so great a throng of raging men. Stephen, therefore, so that he might deserve to receive the crown of his name, had love for arms, and through it he conquered everywhere. Through the love of God he did not yield to the raging Jews; through the love of neighbour he interceded for those stoning [him]. Through love he rebuked those in error, that they might be corrected; through love he prayed for those stoning [him], that they might not be punished. Supported by the strength of love, he conquered Saul, who raged cruelly, and him whom he had as persecutor on earth he deserved to have as companion in heaven. That holy and unwearied love desired to gain by praying those whom it could not convert by admonishing. For, brothers, we must not suppose that Stephen loved his enemies when he prayed for them, and did not love them when he reproved their unbelief by rebuking it. Far be this from the soul of the martyr hastening to the palace of heaven. For the same holy love that kept firm patience in prayer held stern severity in rebuke. And therefore his gentleness deserved to be heard in prayer, because his severity in rebuke was not without love: and so, whether by praying or by rebuking, blessed Stephen preserved love, because in both he had in mind the salvation of those in error, and by the evidence of his holy prayer he showed that that reproof was not of hatred, but of love.

4. In doing this, the blessed martyr both showed love to those present and left a most useful example to those after. For he demonstrated the twofold diligence of the steward of the Church: that, to correct the error of anyone who sins, rebuke should not be lacking in the mouth, and prayer should be poured out humbly to God for him. So that he who has done evil may be put to shame for his evil works by reproof, and may be helped before God by prayer; and thus love itself both sounds justice in the mouth, to correct the one who errs, and keeps patience in the heart, to pour out prayer for the one who errs with a pure affection of love. For he who does not rebuke one who errs is judged for negligence; but he who does not pray for him is condemned for [his] ruin. Therefore, brothers, if ever anyone is rebuked for the salvation of his soul, let him not receive the admonitions of love with disdain; nor let him attend to the present sadness of his own will, but let him consider what gains of profit he acquires. For he is reproved for this reason, that he may be corrected from wicked works. Nor yet, when he sees the rebuke burning with some harshness of words, let him suppose that love is growing cold in the heart. For rebuke is so awake in the mouth that prayer does not sleep in the heart. And so the sinner is wisely provided for in both ways, so that while the man rebuked is put to shame for his sin, he may both be separated from evil works and be saved through prayer (God showing mercy). For holy Scripture also says: For whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he scourges every son whom he receives (Prov. 3:12).

5. Compelled, therefore, by the love of Christ, we both exhort the good to remain in the good, and urge the wicked to depart from evil: especially since in these two saints a twofold sign of salvation is shown to us: that if anyone is good, he should imitate the perseverance of love in Stephen; but whoever is wicked should follow the example of conversion in Paul; and whoever is good should hold to righteousness to the end; but whoever is wicked should depart as quickly as possible from his perversity; let not presumption of righteousness make the good man negligent, nor consideration of his iniquity make the wicked man despair, but let the one hold firmly to the good, the other swiftly forsake evil. Let the good fear lest he fall; let the wicked strive to rise. Whoever, then, is wicked, let him be thrown down with Paul in evil, so that with him he may be raised up in good: for he too fell wicked and rose good. The unjust man was thrown down, and the just man was raised up; the most savage persecutor fell, and the truthful preacher rose. Falling, the impious man lost the light of the body; but rising, justified, he received the light of the heart. And so he was joined to Stephen; from a wolf he was made a sheep. And behold, now Paul rejoices with Stephen, with Stephen enjoys the glory of Christ, with Stephen exults, with Stephen reigns. For where Stephen went before, slain by the stones of Paul, there Paul followed, helped by the prayers of Stephen.

6. What a true life, my brothers! where Paul is not put to shame over the killing of Stephen, but Stephen rejoices over the companionship of Paul, since love rejoices in both. For love in Stephen overcame the savagery of the Jews; love in Paul covered a multitude of sins; love in both alike deserved to possess the kingdom of heaven. Love, therefore, is the fount and origin of all good things, an excellent defence, the way that leads to heaven. Whoever walks in love can neither go astray nor be afraid. It directs, it protects, it leads through. Therefore, brothers, since Christ has set up the ladder of love, by which every Christian can climb up to heaven, hold firmly to pure love, show it to one another, and climb by advancing in it. Persevere in good works, so that you may attain the eternal rewards, helped by the grace of the Saviour, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON IV.
On the Epiphany, and on the Slaughter of the Innocents, and the Gifts of the Magi.

1. You know, dearest brothers, that this day, which is celebrated by us every year in honour of the Lord, is reverently called Epiphany by the mouth of all the faithful. And because it is shown to be a Greek word, it is unknown to many Latins. Hence it is that all Latins indeed say this name, but not all are found to know what they say. Accordingly it is good that all who call today's day Epiphany, and do not know why it is so called, should learn the mystery of this day from the interpretation of its name. For the solemnity of this day ought to be celebrated by the faithful, and therefore the reason for the solemnity ought not to be unknown. This day, then, as we have said, the Christian religion calls Epiphany. And Epiphany is interpreted as Manifestation. We hold it as handed down from the Fathers that the Only-begotten of God, after he was born in time according to the flesh, on this day was manifested to the Magi as they came, by whom, having offered gifts, he was humbly adored. For since he is the God who in the Old Testament (Exod. 25:2) commanded firstfruits to be offered to him, the same God, born man, dedicated the firstfruits of the gentiles to his worship. And apostolic authority testifies that there is one God who justifies the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith (Rom. 3:30): by the name of circumcision undoubtedly indicating the Jews, by the name of uncircumcision the gentiles.

2. These are the two walls which came from opposite sides, and met in unity of faith in the stone which has become the head of the corner. One wall came from the Jews, the other came from the gentiles. They were far apart from each other when they believed different things: the cornerstone was placed in the middle, to draw both walls to itself and to call both by one name, so that those who were made one in the one grace of the sacrament might be one by sharing the name. For through Christ, who is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2:14), Jews and gentiles were made one, on whom the unity of faith bestowed the one name of Christian. To the cornerstone, then, each wall came, and the unity of faith made a true corner. Of these two walls one was brought when the angel announced to the Jewish shepherds that Christ was born; the other wall was brought when a new star appeared to the gentile Magi.

3. The former were the firstfruits of the Jews; the latter were made the firstfruits of the gentiles; the former brought from nearby, the latter led back from afar. For the Jews, who worshipped God, were near; the gentiles, who served idols, were far off. This indeed was signified by the shepherds, who were found nearby when Christ was born, and by the Magi, who were brought from distant parts. Yet these, on coming, though they themselves were not Jews, declared that they were seeking the king of the Jews, and said they had come to adore him. For the evangelist says that Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who is born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East, and have come to adore him (Matt. 2:1-2). Why is it, sweetest brothers, that these Magi sought the king of the Jews to adore, though they themselves were not Jews? And what king? Certainly not Herod, but Christ. They wish to adore a king newly born, and do not adore a king appointed some years before. They desire to adore a suckling infant, and do not adore a king ruling over peoples. For sons had already been born to Herod, king of the Jews, who were to reign when their father died. For when this Herod died, Archelaus reigned in Judaea, and the younger Herod obtained the principality of Galilee.

4. Archelaus was born in a palace, Christ in a lodging-place. Archelaus, when born, was laid in a silver bed; but Christ, when born, was placed in a very narrow manger. The one was perhaps wrapped in costly silks, the other was wrapped in the cheapest cloths. And yet the one born in a palace is disregarded; the one born in a lodging-place is sought. The one is not named by the Magi at all; the other, once found, is humbly adored. The king's firstborn is utterly passed over, and the firstborn of a poor little woman is adored with gifts. Who is this king of the Jews, poor and rich, lowly and exalted? Who is this king of the Jews who is carried as a little child and adored as God? Little in a manger, boundless in heaven; mean in his cloths, precious in the stars: on learning of whose birth Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (ibid., 3).

5. Why are you so troubled, Herod? Because you have heard that the king of the Jews is born, you are troubled, you are tossed by suspicions, you are inflamed by the goads of envy, and for this reason you try to kill the newborn king. This trouble of yours is empty, and your plotting utterly vain. This king who is born did not come to overcome kings by fighting, but to subdue them wonderfully by admonishing; nor was he born to succeed you, but so that the world might faithfully believe in him. For he came not to fight while living, but to triumph when slain; not to seek an army for himself from other nations with gold, but to pour out his precious blood to save the nations. In vain, through envy, you feared as a successor the one whom, through believing, you ought to have sought as saviour: for if you believed in him, you would reign with him; and just as you received a temporal kingdom from him, you would receive an everlasting one too. For this child's kingdom is not of this world, but through him there is reigning in the world. For he is the Wisdom of God, which says in Proverbs: Through me kings reign (Prov. 8:15). This child is the Word of God, this child is the Power and Wisdom of God. If you can, [...] against the Wisdom of God [...]. You are turning to your own ruin, and do not know it. For you would never have had a kingdom had you not received it from this child who has now (or: then) been born. The child who is now called by the Magi King of the Jews is likewise the Creator and Lord of the angels. Therefore, since you fear the infancy of the one being born, you ought rather to fear the omnipotence of the one who judges. Do not fear him as the successor to your kingdom, but fear him as the most just condemner of your unbelief.

6. Would that, while the Magi adored him, you too had adored him likewise, and had not sent the Magi to him with deceitful cunning! Go, he says, and inquire diligently about the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and adore him (Matt. 2:8). O feigned cunning! O impious unbelief! O deceitful wickedness! If you most certainly intended to adore this child, why did you kill many children on his account? The blood of the innocents, which you cruelly shed, bears witness to what you wanted concerning this child. And yet not only did you not find this child, but you did no harm at all to those children: rather, unknowingly, you did what was to their profit. For through your savagery those became martyrs who through their infancy had been innocent: since through the grace of this child they were found worthy to die for him before they could confess him before men. This child, then, who created the world, who rules the world, who does whatever he wills, who arranges all things in a wonderful and unsurpassable order, ordained this and brought this about: that through your raging envy those children should receive a precious death, and that what you could not provide for them as a friend for your salvation (or: their salvation), this you should do as an enemy for your damnation. For this purpose, then, he allowed you to kill the infants, that he might make them triumph over you. He let you go on to wickedness; he led them on to the palm. For one and the same is the almighty Lord and the crying little child; one and the same is he who deigned to flee your cruelty and whose majesty you cannot escape. For he fled not from human fear but by divine dispensation; he fled not of necessity but by power. And he deigned to flee into Egypt for this reason, that afterwards he might deign to mount the cross; and by that power by which the child lay hidden in Egypt, by that power the young man hung on the wood. For one and the same is he who undertook death and he who bestows life: one and the same, immortal from the Father, mortal from his mother; dying by his own power, rising by his own power.

7. This child who is born, then, is not found among the number of the little ones who die, because he is the expectation of the nations. The blood of this child is therefore (or: accordingly) not shed with the blood of these children, because it alone is to be shed for the remission of sins; and all those children would die in vain, were they not saved by this one's blood. And this child will most certainly die, for if he were unwilling to die, he would never have been born. But he will die not to fulfil your savagery, but to complete his own gentleness: for his own kindness will make him die, not another's malice. He will die not so that you, an unbeliever, may reign in the world, but so that he may make the faithful reign with him in heaven. He will die not to lose a kingdom, but to win those who will reign. He will die not to lose a brief life, but to bestow an everlasting one. He will die not as a slave of iniquity, but as the Lord of majesty. He will die not by the chain of necessity, but by the purpose of his will. He will die wonderfully, he will die mercifully, he will die uniquely, he will die by his own power, so that he may fulfil his will in all things. For he will die mercifully to this end, that rising again he may rule over all nations. He will die, then, as one [and the same], namely he whom, God and man, the faith of a virgin conceived, and whom, God and man, virginal fruitfulness brought forth.

8. If you do not know the true deity of this child, look at the star shining in the sky, going before the Magi and showing the way to those who did not know it. This star never appeared before, because this child has now created it, and appointed it to go before the Magi as they came to him. This child is indeed laid in a manger as a little one, but he works wonderfully as great in heaven. He allows himself to be carried in hands on earth, but he commands heavenly things to serve him. Why is it, then, that you look at his infant age and do not understand his divine power? Thus the natural divinity and the natural humanity of this child had to be truly made known, each by nature true, both united, neither confused with each other nor separated from each other. For Mary had as her son, born of her, the very one to whom a star rendered the service it owed. Mary in Bethlehem brought forth as God (or: Lord) and man the very same one whom the star announced to the Magi in the East. So the Magi came, and recognised the Virgin's son as one and the same God (or: Lord) and man.

9. Then look at what they offered, and recognise what they believed. For the evangelist relates that, entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother: and falling down they adored him; and opening their treasures they offered him gifts, gold, frankincense and myrrh (Matt. 2:11). Through these three kinds of gifts, in one and the same Christ are made known the divine majesty, the royal power, and human mortality. For frankincense pertains to sacrifice, gold to tribute, myrrh to the burial of the dead. All these holy faith does not cease truly to offer to Christ, as it believes him to be one and the same true God, true king and true man, and truly acknowledges that he truly died for us.

10. In the offering of frankincense the Arian is confounded, who contends that sacrifice ought to be offered to the Father alone: in the offering of myrrh the Manichaean is confounded, who does not believe that Christ truly died for our salvation: and in the gold both are confounded together, since the Manichaean does not believe in a king born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and the Arian strives to ascribe a natural servitude to the Only-begotten God. Accordingly neither will experience him as a king by whom he is ruled (or: reigned over) through faith, but as one by whom he is punished for the crime of unbelief: for by the one the truth of the divinity, by the other the truth of the flesh, is denied. By these same gifts Nestorius too is confounded, who strives to divide Christ into two persons: for he sees that the Magi humbly offered the same gifts, not some to God and others to the man, but to the one God and man. Let him not, then, be divided in persons who is not found divided in the gifts. For indeed one and the same is honoured with these gifts so that one and the same may be recognised as God and man. This offering of the Magi also confounds the madness of Eutyches, who will not proclaim both true natures in Christ. For he takes away the truth of these gifts when he contends for proclaiming one nature in Christ.

11. So let us, dearly beloved brothers, offer to Christ without doubting in faith what the Magi are known to have offered in gift: so that the confession of true divinity and humanity may itself be our faithful offering before Christ. Let us offer these gifts with one mind together with the Magi, and let us make for the country of the saints with the whole devotion of the heart. And let us not keep to the way of the old life, but humbly obeying the divine commandments, let us change our way and walk in the way (or: and walk as) the Lord has commanded, so that we may be able to reach the homeland, where we may rejoice without end with the Lord himself. For a man's way is his life. Whoever lives badly keeps to the way of error; whoever lives well walks along the way of truth. Therefore whoever used to walk the way of fornication, let him keep to the way of chastity; whoever used to keep to the way of avarice, let him keep to the way of mercy; whoever used to walk along the way of pretence, let him now keep to the way of purity. Let us walk well by faith, so that we may come to sight (or: hope), where our joy will be full, because our desire will be filled with good things, through him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON 5.
On the love of God and of neighbour.

1. The more I long to pay your holiness the sermon I owe on love, the more I see myself becoming a greater debtor of love; and I do not find how I could set out in words the praise of love, in which, as long as we live in this world, we ought to grow in loving one another, just as we are commanded always to owe it by paying it. For the blessed apostle Paul, when he had commanded that we be released from all debts, wished us always to be held by the one debt of mutual love, saying: Owe no one anything, except to love one another (Rom. 13:8). This is the sum of the apostolic teaching. These are the counsels of fatherly love: that we owe no one anything, except to love one another. So when we hear that we should owe no one anything, let us not stop at this word, but let us hear and do what follows, that we love one another: and we shall find holy love, which we may pay by always owing, and owe to our salvation by paying. A great thing is love, dearly beloved brothers, which, as the Apostle teaches, we are commanded always to pay in such a way that we are nonetheless commanded to owe it without ceasing. O debt of love, a good debt, a holy debt, a debt filled with heavenly benefits, a debt wholly full of everlasting riches!

2. Great gains, brothers, do we acquire by this debt; immense benefits do we obtain by such interest. For while love is paid and owed by us, all our iniquity is forgiven and blotted out. Indeed blessed David begged that this very love be given back to him to blot out his iniquities, when he was tearfully entreating the Lord for a grievous sin. For when, once taken captive by an enticing sight, he committed adultery with the wife of his soldier, and, doubling the crime, also killed the innocent husband, after committing the sin he was rebuked by the oracle through the prophet, and after confession was restored by a healing reply; and while, prostrate in suppliant entreaty, he poured out words of penitence by which to appease as quickly as possible the just God, the King of kings and Lord of lords, he is known to have said among other things: Turn away your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities (Ps. 50:11); and since he saw that this could not be done without the gift of love, he at once added: Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me (ibid. 12). That a clean heart is the dwelling of love the Apostle commends in these words, saying: For the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned (1 Tim. 1:5).

3. Accordingly two things in these words of the prophet must be carefully considered by us: one that he asked to be taken away from him, the other that he requested to be granted to him. For he asked that his iniquities be blotted out, and that a clean heart be created in him and a right spirit renewed within him. And what is iniquity, if not depraved desire? And what is cleanness of heart, if not holy love of God and of neighbour? So when the prophet says: Turn away your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities, and immediately adds: Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me, what else did he say but: Blot out from me the stain of depraved desire, and give me the grace of love? Take from me desire, through which I may be condemned; and give me love, through which I may deserve to be crowned. Take from me desire, on account of which there is grief and groaning without ceasing in torment; and give me love, through which there is reigning without end in heaven. For if I have love, which I pay by owing and owe by paying, I shall not fear iniquity, for which I would pay without end in grief. Rightly, then, does the Apostle command that we owe no one anything, except to love one another: for by this debt the heap of all offences is taken from us, because love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8). But let no one think, brothers, that love must be paid by us in such a way that, once paid, it at some time ceases to be owed. For when it is paid, more is owed; and it is acquired the more, the more it is paid while it is owed. For whoever does not think himself always a debtor of love, let him not rejoice that he is released from the debt, but mourn that he is bereft of the gift of love. For he does not have the love he has ceased to have, because as a prodigal debtor he lost by not paying what he received so as always to pay it and always have it. Therefore let him know that he has lost what he had received when he has not paid what he owed.

4. But someone says: To whom do I owe this? Or to whom must I pay this love? We answer that love must be paid to all men, that is, to known and unknown, to good and bad, to friends and enemies. For when the blessed Apostle says: Therefore while we have time, let us do what is good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith (Gal. 6:10), he clearly shows that in the work of love one person is indeed to be preferred to others (or: to another), yet no one is to be excluded from the benefits of love. So that holy, pure love, and, to speak properly, Christian love, which is patient, which is kind, which is not envious, which does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, which is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth, which bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, love which never fails (1 Cor. 13:4ff.), should so (perhaps: thus) embrace friends as to extend even to enemies: let it give itself to friends who are willing, press itself on enemies who are unwilling; let it keep the former, win the latter; let it delight the former, so that from friends they do not become enemies; let it invite the latter, so that from enemies they become friends.

5. Let us remember, brothers, the words of the Lord who says: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you (Matt. 5:44). See, the Lord commands love to be extended even to enemies, and the goodwill of the Christian heart to be widened even to persecutors. And what reward will be given for such great works? Or what gift is bestowed on those who obey this precept? Let him show the reward prepared by him for love, who through the Holy Spirit deigns freely to pour in love itself: let him tell us what he will give in return for love to the worthy, who deigns to give that same love to the unworthy. Let the Lord speak, then, let him speak, and in his own words show us the greatness of his promise: So that you may be, he says, sons of your Father who is in heaven (ibid. 45). For when he commanded enemies to be loved, what was enjoined on the hearer was perhaps bitter: let what is promised to the obedient, I beg, be sweet. Let the delight of this sweetness, then, be held in the heart, and the difficulty of that bitterness will be overcome. For those who love their enemies, and do good to those who hate them, will be sons of God.

6. What these sons of God will receive the Apostle declares, saying: The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. And if sons, heirs also: heirs of God, and co-heirs with Christ (Rom. 8:16-17). Hear then, Christians; hear, sons of God; hear, heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. That you may possess the fatherly inheritance, spend love not only on friends but also on enemies. Let love be denied to no one, which is possessed in common by good men (perhaps: by all). All of you have it together, and so that you may have it more, spend it on both good and bad. For this is the common possession of the good, not earthly but heavenly; and therefore the person of a sharer causes no one to be straitened in it. Love increases as much as desire has been diminished; and love makes always free the one whom worldly desire has not held captive. Love is the gift of God, as the Apostle says: The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). Desire is the snare of the devil, not only a snare but also a sword: by it he catches the wretched, by it he kills those caught. Love is the root of all goods, desire is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10). Desire is always tormented, since it is not healed by seizing. But love always rejoices, since the more it is multiplied, the more lavishly it is given out. And therefore, just as the seeker of iniquity grows poor by acquiring, so the payer of love grows rich by paying. Desire is troubled while it seeks to avenge injury; love is calm while it delights to forgive.
566 SERMON VI.
On the holy martyr Cyprian.

1. The bright birthday of so great a martyr, namely the blessed Cyprian, on which, stripped of his earthly and dying limbs, he passed over to the rewards of eternal life, has commended to us both the teaching of his priesthood and the victory of his martyrdom, and has made [this day] freer from the sadness it once held for a time. For while the bishop suffered by confessing, between the danger of a bloody death and the glory of a devoted contest, the Church suffered with him by praying. Who does not know, or rather who does not recognise by prudent reflection, that this very day, which now comes round to us as a feast in its yearly return, was at that time anxious for Christian and religious minds? Then, when the bishop had taken up the summit [of the struggle] against the devil, the devout expectation of the people trembled, that faith might so resist the persecutor that the flesh would not give way to the flatterer; that the shepherd might so go before as not to desert the fold, and the wolf (God forbid) invade it once deserted. The Church grieved that so very illustrious a priest was meanwhile withdrawn from its fellowship: but yet it rejoiced that, with Christ's adversary laid low, the martyr had come out victor. His praiseworthy teaching was in their memory, his wonderful courage was before their eyes, when so great a [man of] God kept what he had taught, and showed what the rest ought to do, no longer by words but by deeds, confirming the faithfulness of his sermons with the examples of his acts, with firm solidity, believing and trusting that Christ died for the salvation of all, and that he himself should not withdraw from being killed for his name. For by whose blood he had once been redeemed though unworthy, for him he poured out his own blood, now worthy; and from him whose blood he had faithfully drunk in this life he had believed that eternal life could be given back to him.

2. For he who had given the law gave them a blessing, so that they might walk from strength to strength: from the strength of most sincere faith to the strength of most constant combat; from the strength of most ardent love to the strength of most glorious suffering. For he believed, [therefore] he spoke; he loved, and he followed. For he had heard the Lord say: Whoever loves me follows me (John 6:26); and again: Whoever believes in me will not die for ever. And the faithful father (or: likewise faithful) followed the footsteps of the Saviour. Undaunted, he scorned the commands of princes and the edict of judges. Ready, he received the blow of the executioner, and death itself kept unconquered the mind subject to God alone. In short, nothing called him back from the care of shepherd and flock: not the place of exile, the violent officer, the time of persecution, fear of the judge, the sword hanging over him, the approaching end of death. For even when placed in exile, and separated from the Church entrusted to him in body only, not in mind, he kept up the feeding of the poor; when hidden in concealment, the strictness of discipline; when held by the prince, the chastity of the virgins; when brought before the tribunal, 567 the protection of the clergy; when driven by threats, a robust conscience; when craftily worn down, spiritual caution; when unjustly judged, Christian patience. Admonishing the people with frequent letters, he cherished the needy with more generous alms, urged the martyrs on to undertake the battle by exhortations and examples alike, and until he lays down his life he does not abandon his charge.

3. In short, he is guarded and he guards, a carefree despiser of his own pain, an anxious preserver of others' modesty, fearing lust more than sorrow, and more wary of the devil's enticements than afraid of many torments. For the faith he keeps watch against the roaring lion, for chastity he fights against the hissing [serpent]. He conquers in his own body the wickedness of the raging one, in the flesh of the girls the softness of the flatterer; trampling on the threats of the persecutor, he avoids the deceit of the deceiver; he neither yields in anything to the furious one, nor allowed the violent one to steal anything. Therefore, considering his struggle, his perseverance, his victory and his crown alike, and refreshing in the sweet mirror of the mind what he escaped and where he arrived, let us sing with yearly devotion: Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. The snare is broken, and we are set free (Ps. 123:6, 7).
SERMON VII.
On the thief crucified with Christ.

1. We celebrate the Lord's Pasch, a mystery wonderful above the other holy festivals, and to be revered. For Pascha in Hebrew is rendered in Latin 'Passing-over'. Our iniquity had shut off this passage, until it was opened by the key of the cross. For our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ had indeed mortal flesh, but did not have a sinful soul. By taking on punishment without guilt, he made guilt pass away without punishment. At his passion all the stars were shaken, and the elements trembled at the event of the Lord's wound. The day was terrified at an unaccustomed night, and the world found a darkness not its own. The day stood shut in under an uncertain light, and the very light of the world almost seemed to die with God. For this reason, namely, all brightness passed into night, so that it would not be forced to look upon the sacrilege. For heaven had closed its eyes, so as not to see the Lord on the cross. And the world itself did not deserve to be a witness, so that only he who struck might see. The persecutor struck with the lance, and the Redeemer poured out our price. For when the Lord suffered, all the apostles fled, all abandoned him. Where is that crowd which went before the Lord, that crowd, I say, which said: Hosanna to the son of David, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (Matt. 1:29)?

2. The Lord suffered, and all fled. All became mute, lukewarm in love, crushed by fear; a little later they flee. Others, then, did not recognise him when he was working miracles; the thief recognised him hanging on the cross, 568 though nailed in all his limbs. His hands nailed, his feet nailed, all his limbs nailed. His whole body was fixed on the cross, and yet his tongue confessed Christ. Now there was one place for the three crucified: in the middle the Lord, who was reckoned among the wicked (Isa. 53:12): they placed two thieves on this side and that, but they did not have a similar case. They were joined to the sides of the one hanging, but they were far separated. Their own crimes crucified them; our sins crucified Christ. But in one of them it appeared plainly enough how much avails not the torment of one hanging but the devotion of one confessing. The thief gained in pain what Peter had lost in fear. He committed a crime, mounted the cross, changed his case, purchased paradise. He fully deserved to change his case, who did not despise in Christ the likeness of punishment. The Jews despised him when he worked miracles; this man believed in him as he hung. He recognised the Lord as his partner on the cross, and the violent thief by believing did violence to the kingdom of heaven. The thief believed in Christ at the moment when the apostolic faith trembled. Rightly he deserved to hear: Today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). For this he had certainly not promised himself. He commended himself indeed to great mercy, but he also considered his own deserts. Lord, he said (v. 42), remember me when you come into your kingdom. Until the Lord should come into his kingdom, he expected that he would be in punishment, and begged that at least at his coming mercy might be shown to him.

3. So the thief, considering his own deserts, put it off; but the Lord offered the thief what he had despaired of, as if he were saying: You ask that I remember you when I come into my kingdom, and I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise. Recognise to whom you commend yourself, whom you believe will come. Before I come, I am everywhere. Therefore, although I am about to descend into hell, I will have you today with me in paradise, not entrusted to another, but with me. For my lowliness descended to mortal men and to the dead themselves; but my divinity never departed from paradise. So there were made three crosses, three cases: one of the thieves mocked Christ; the other, confessing his wrongs, commended himself to Christ's mercy. The cross of Christ in the middle was not a punishment but a tribunal. It condemned the mocker, it freed the believer. Fear, you who mock; rejoice, you who believe. May Christ do in glory what he did in lowliness. Divine gifts come from a deep judgement. We can marvel at them; but we cannot search them out, nor explain them.
569 SERMON VIII.
On the holy day of Pentecost.

1. The yearly solemnity is held of the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ sent the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, whom he had promised to the disciples beforehand. For he had said: He cannot come unless I go away (John 16:7). And so on the fortieth day after his resurrection, whose solemnity we kept ten days ago, he ascended into heaven, and, not forgetful of his promise, today he sent the Holy Spirit, whom he had promised, to the hundred and twenty who had gathered together and were faithfully awaiting at last the Lord's promise. They spoke in all tongues. For so it pleased God at that time to signify the presence of the Holy Spirit, that whoever had received him spoke in all tongues. So first let us briefly see why, when he promised him, he said: He cannot come unless I go away. For the Holy Spirit is not separable from the Son of God, nor was he unable to come while he was present, from whom he cannot depart. But since the Lord was still showing the weak disciples the form of a servant, in which the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us; and the form of a servant (text: cause; perhaps: form), that is, the Lord's flesh, even the carnal could look upon; but the form of God, in which he did not think it robbery to be equal to God (Phil. 2:6), can be conceived only by the spiritual; for this reason he said: He cannot come unless I go away, as if he were saying: As long as your carnal affection is occupied with my flesh, so long your spiritual gaze does not take in my divinity. For he had promised that by the gift of the Holy Spirit they would be led into all truth, as it is written: Cleansing their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9). And blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt. 6:8). So the bodily form of the Lord withdrew from their bodily eyes, so that through the Holy Spirit the Lord's divinity might be instilled into their hearts.

4. Now let us next see why at that time this was the sign of the Holy Spirit's presence, that those who had received him spoke in all tongues. For even now the Holy Spirit is still given, and yet those who receive him do not speak in all tongues, the evident miracle by which he showed himself at that time. It must be understood, dearest brothers, that this is the Holy Spirit through whom love is poured out in our hearts. And since love was going to gather the Church of God throughout the whole world, as then even one man receiving the Holy Spirit could speak in all tongues, so now the very unity of the Church, gathered by the Holy Spirit, speaks in all tongues. So if anyone says to one of us: You have received the Holy Spirit, why do you not speak in all tongues? he ought to answer: I do indeed speak in all tongues, because I am in the body of Christ, that is, in the Church, which speaks in all tongues. For what else did God signify then through the presence of the Holy Spirit, except that his Church would speak in all tongues? 570 So what the Lord had promised was fulfilled: No one puts new wine into old wineskins, but they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved (Matt. 9:17). Rightly, then, when they were heard speaking in all tongues, some said: These men are full of new wine (Acts 2:12). For they had already been made new wineskins, renewed by the grace of holiness, so that, filled with new wine, that is, with the Holy Spirit, they glowed as they spoke in all tongues, and by that most evident miracle they foreshadowed the Catholic Church that was to be, through the tongues of all nations. And for this reason heretics are rightly believed not to have the Holy Spirit, since they are divided from the body which has been found worthy to sound forth in all tongues throughout all nations.

5. So celebrate this day as members of the unity of the body of Christ. For you do not celebrate in vain if you are what you celebrate: holding fast to that Church which the Lord, filling it with the Holy Spirit, recognises as his own as it grows through the whole world, and by which he is recognised as its own. As a bridegroom he has not lost his own bride; no one substitutes another's for him. For to you, established among all nations, that is, to the Church of Christ, the members of Christ, the body of Christ, the bride of Christ, the Apostle says: Bearing with one another in love, eager to keep with one another the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:2-3). See that where he commanded that we bear with one another, there he placed love; where he named the hope of unity, there he showed the bond of peace. This is the house of God built of living stones, in which such a father of the household may delight to dwell, whose eyes the ruin of division ought not to offend.
SERMON IX.
On Saint Vincent.

1. I wonder, brothers, whether you still want to hear anything. For after so great a passion of martyrdom as has just been read to us, the speaker is superfluous and the listener wearied. For just now there was read to us of a savage judge, a bloody torturer, and an unconquered martyr: on whose body, furrowed by various punishments, the torments had already given out, and still the limbs endured. Impiety, refuted by so many miracles, persisted; weakness, harassed by so many tortures, did not yield; the hidden divinity was recognised. For when would corruptible dust hold out against such monstrous torments, unless Christ dwelt in it? I certainly, brothers, after so great a spectacle, which the course of the reading as it ran presented to our minds, would not entrust my sermon to your ears, were it not that my mouth speaks the praise of the Lord (Ps. 144:21). In all these things, then, he is to be recognised, he is to be glorified, he is to be praised, who gave both faith at the first calling and strength in the final passion. Do you wish to know that both were given? Hear the apostle Paul: To you, he says, it has been given by Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him (Phil. 1:29). Vincent had received both of these. 571 He had received, therefore he had. For if he had not received, what would he have had? He had confidence in speech, he had endurance in suffering. So let no one presume on his own heart when he utters speech. Let no one trust in his own strength when he endures temptation. For even that we may speak good things prudently, our wisdom is from him.

2. Recall the Lord Christ admonishing his disciples in the Gospel. Recall the King of martyrs equipping his cohorts with spiritual arms, showing them the battles, supplying aid, promising rewards. When he had said to his disciples: In this world you will have distress (John 16:33), at once, to console them in their fright, he added: But have confidence, for I have conquered the world (ibid.). Why then do we wonder, dearest brothers, if Vincent conquered in him by whom the world was conquered? In this world, he says, you will have distress. Though it presses, it does not crush; though it assails, it does not take by storm. The world brings out a double battle line against the soldiers of Christ. For it flatters so as to deceive, it terrifies so as to break. Let our own will not hold us, and let another's cruelty not terrify us. Let Christ meet both approaches, and the Christian is not conquered. If you consider that in this passion the strength was human, it begins to be incredible; if it is recognised to have been divine, it is recognised as wonderful. So great a cruelty raged on the martyr's body, and so great a calm came forth in his voice. So harsh were the many punishments raging in his limbs, and so great a serenity sounded in his words.

3. In a wondrous way we might think that while Vincent suffered another was speaking, or surely that while Vincent spoke another was being tortured. And truly, brothers, so it was, entirely so it was: another was speaking. For Christ promised this too to his witnesses. You heard it just now. He was speaking in the Gospel, and saying to his own, whom he was preparing for contests of this kind: Do not think how or what you are to speak. For it will be given you in that hour how or what you are to speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt. 10:19-20). So the flesh suffered, the spirit spoke. And as the spirit spoke, not only was impiety refuted, but weakness too was strengthened. The torments made the martyr more glorious to us. Pierced by a manifold variety of wounds, he did not abandon the fight, but renewed it more fiercely. You would think that the flame hardened rather than burned; and that, like a potter's kiln receiving soft clay, it rendered it hard earth. Our martyr could have said to Datianus: My flesh no longer cares for your fires, because my strength has dried up like a potsherd (Ps. 21:16). For it is truly written: The kiln tests the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation just men (Ecclus. 27:6). Vincent was tested and baked in that fire. But Datianus burned and cracked. For if he was not burning, why was he smoking? What were the words of the angry man but the smoke of one burning? So he applied flames from outside to our martyr, who had refreshment in his heart; but he himself, kindled by the torches of fury, burned within like an oven, and consumed his inhabitant, the devil. For through the furious cries of Datianus that you heard, through his fierce eyes and threatening looks, through the turbulent movements of his whole body, that inner inhabitant of his was stirring, and through these visible signs, as 572 through the cracking crevices of the little vessel he had filled, he was betrayed. The flame did not torment the martyr so much as madness ravaged him.

4. But now, brothers, all those things have passed, both the wrath of Datianus and the punishment of Vincent. Yet punishment remains for Datianus, a crown for Vincent. Indeed, to show, leaving aside for the moment the ends of the tribulation to come, the glory of the martyrs even in this world: what region today, what province overseas, as far as either the Roman empire or the Roman name extends, does not rejoice to celebrate the birthday of Vincent? But who today would even have heard the name of Datianus, had he not read it in this passion? And that the Lord preserved the martyr's body with such care, as you heard, what else did it show, except that he had guided him as he conquered, whom he did not abandon when lifeless? So Vincent conquered Datianus living, and conquered him dead too: living he trampled on torments, dead he swam across seas. But he who amid the hooks gave him an unconquered mind himself steered the lifeless corpse amid the waves. The torturer's flame did not bend his heart, the sea's water did not sink his body; but in all these things nothing is his, except that precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints (Ps. 115:15).
SERMON X.
On what the prophet Micah says: I will show you, O man, what is good.

1. On the present prophetic reading, in which great profit for our souls is contained, we have resolved to speak to your charity, asking a fitting power of speech from him from whom we freely received a good will. For who gives this, except God, who works in his own both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will (Phil. 2:13)? So let us together go over the words of holy Micah which we heard together. And would, brothers, that as we go over them in speech, so we may fulfil them in works! For we heard the words of a holy man, a just man, a devout man, a man anxious for his salvation, a man who knew he was created by God, who considered that he was under God: who with great fear and trembling awaited the divine judgment, in which he knew he would render account before the tribunal of the just Judge not only for his deeds and words, but even for his very thoughts. So, thinking on the coming judgment of God, which all of us too ought to fear and think on with great dread of heart in all our works: thinking on this, this holy and just man asked what he should do, or with what gifts he might entreat God the judge. But he knew that almighty God, who founded all things, who made all things from nothing, who established nothing out of the need of poverty, but all things 573 out of the abundance of goodness, seeks not our gifts alone, but also our works. Rather, he knew that God delights in our gifts most of all in this, that we please him with holy conduct and good works.
