So, asking what should be offered by man to God, this man said: What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord (Mic. 6:6)? And by this word, in which he does not say, What shall I offer to the Lord? but, What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord? he taught us that if ever we wish to offer a gift to God, we should seek something worthy, and offer that. But what can be worthy of God in an offering, except what is foremost in creation? And among all the creatures which the Lord made upon the earth, none better can be found than that creature which God made in his own image. And this creature on earth is man.

2. Whoever, then, wishes to offer something worthy to God offers nothing else before himself; for God, who made man in his own image, delights that his own image be offered to him, and commands that it be presented to him pure and clean. That is why our Saviour answered certain men who were testing him thus: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's (Matt. 22:21). That is to say: O man, just as you render to Caesar his image on the coin, so render to God his image in yourself. Render, O man, to your creator his image; render it just, not wicked; render it humble, not proud: not foul with avarice, not disfigured by rapacity, not made fickle by the vice of anger, not crushed by love of earthly things, not soiled by envy, not polluted by fornication; but whole by the weight of prudence, clean by the truth of faith, and resplendent with good conduct and works. And how we are to render to God his image in us, the most holy prophet admonishes, saying: I will show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord seeks from you. Surely, to do judgement, and justice, and to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God (Mic. 6:8).

3. First, then, let us inquire what it is to do judgement, which the blessed prophet put first. A judgement is the name for an assembly where the accusation and defence of some person is conducted: whence it must be that he who is guilty goes out condemned, and he who is proved innocent departs the victor. Return, then, to yourself, O man. Seek the accusation in yourself, seek the defence in yourself, seek the judgement in yourself. Rather, be yourself accuser, and defender, and judge. Enter into the inner chamber of your heart, where the eyes of the Lord your God alone see you. There accuse yourself, so that you may be defended by the accusation. There convict yourself, so that you may obtain the victory. There condemn yourself, so that you may deserve to be acquitted. There punish yourself, if you wish to be freed from the torment of eternal punishment. Hold in yourself, Christian, a true and right judgement; attend carefully to the secrets of your heart. Set your evil deeds before your own eyes: whatever you had erased, review and reread often in the inmost book of your remembrance; examine yourself, you yourself, without indulgence, and afflict yourself with the tortures of your thoughts. Pronounce a just sentence upon yourself. Whatever evil you had done by sinning, punish truly by repenting; and, made judge of your own sins, do to your iniquities what judges are accustomed to do to those guilty of capital crimes. Do not show partiality to your own 574 person when you judge your own case. But examine your evils with severity, pronounce the sentence of condemnation on your sins with rigour (another reading: vigour), and kill the sins which you condemn in yourself.

4. And this is to kill sins: from then on in no way to obey sins. So do not be a doer of sins, and you will be their slayer. And if you are a just judge over your sins, you will come out acquitted from the just judgement of God. And so that you can hold a just judgement upon yourself, hear the apostle Paul, who teaches which works you ought to mortify in yourself, so that you may come to life. For he says: Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols; on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the sons of unbelief (Col. 3:5-6). See, O man, you have what to judge in yourself, you have what to condemn, what to mortify in yourself. Judge these, and you will not be judged. Condemn these, and you will not be condemned. Mortify these, and you will not die. Here be a most severe judge, here be a most vehement executioner. Judge these by considering them rightly, mortify them by casting them off. For if you have considered your sins rightly, you have judged; if you have cast them off, you have killed [them]. So, to defend yourself, accuse yourself; to acquit yourself, judge yourself; and to bring your case to victory, consider your conscience. Acknowledge your iniquity, mortify your desire, correct your life, and by judging rightly you will set your soul free.

5. See, brothers, as far as the Lord has granted, we have said what it is to do judgement; now let us say what it is, next, to do justice. To do justice is this: that what you do not wish done to you, you do not do to another, but also that you do to another what you are glad to have done to you by another. Now you wish good to be done to you by every person: for this is just, that every person do good to a person; because he acts against justice who does evil to a person. But by evil I mean that deed by which sin is committed through wicked desire, not that by which punishment is inflicted on sinners through love. By evil I now mean, not that by which a neighbour is called back from fault, but that by which the just God is provoked to anger. I mean that evil, not which severity is wont to inflict well, but which iniquity is accustomed to perpetrate wickedly. I now mean that evil which can never be just, but is always found unjust. I mean that evil by which offence is given to God, not by which a neighbour is helped. So I now mean that evil which is evil for all who do it in such a way that it is good for no one who suffers it. A person, then, will do justice if he does evil to no one and does good to all; and let him do to no one that evil from which the blessed Apostle forbids us, saying: Rendering to no one evil for evil (Rom. 12:17). With these words he commended to us complete goodwill. For he did not say: Doing evil to no one, but: Rendering to no one evil for evil, showing that it is little for a Christian not to inflict evil unless he learns also not to repay it. Whence it is recognised how very bad it is if we do evil to anyone, we who, when others do evil, ought not to render evil for evil.

6. Keep justice, then, Christian, according to the rule. Do good 575 to every person; but evil neither do to anyone, nor repay. For if you render evil for evil, you too will without doubt be evil. Then he who first did you evil will not be the only evil one, because he will have you as a partner in malice. And when you begin to render evil for evil, you will be the more culpable in this, that you imitate the evil which you detest in others. And once made evil, you do not conquer evil, but are conquered by evil, and, what is worse, you are conquered not by another's evil but by your own. For there is no way for you to become evil except by falling away from goodness. So it will come about that you remain damnably conquered in yourself, if you are depraved by the vice of your own will. Then, therefore, you will most certainly overcome an evil person, if you yourself remain good, if you render not evils for evils, but goods for evils. For this reason the Apostle, who says: Rendering to no one evil for evil, says a little later: Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good (ibid., 21).

7. See, we have heard together from the Apostle that we should render to no one evil for evil; let us likewise hear again from the same apostle that we should also do good to all, when he says: Therefore, while we have time, let us work good toward all (Gal. 6:10). Then, therefore, we do justice, when we do to people those things which we wish to be done to us by people. Commending this justice, the Saviour himself says: All things whatever you wish that people should do to you, do the same to them also (Matt. 7:12). And what do you wish people to do to you, except good things? But if they do evil things to you, they do not do what you wish. So you too, if you render evil for evil, since you are not doing to people the things you wish them to do to you, are certainly not doing what Christ commanded, but what the devil urged. Therefore, so that you may do the justice which Christ commanded, bestow on each person what you desire to be bestowed on you by all people. Thus you will do judgement and justice, about which the blessed prophet admonished us. For you will do judgement if you condemn your sins by repenting, and by condemning sins live well. And you will do justice if you render to no one evil for evil, but do good things to all people. This the Apostle certainly commends, saying: See that no one renders evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all (1 Thess. 5:15).

8. But since good works are done well and profitably when they proceed from a good will, therefore, when the prophet had said that we ought to do judgement and justice, he added: And to love mercy. For the exalted ought above all to bestow mercy on the lowly, and the rich to bestow it on the poor. Now this mercy is bestowed in two ways: when pardon is given to one who sins and promises amendment, and when what is necessary is not denied to one in need. It belongs to the part of this mercy that the superior not oppress the inferior but defend him with justice, and that the rich man take nothing from the poor man but feed and clothe the poor man; that he not lay snares for the poor man, but rather console him with his kindnesses. Why then does frail and mortal man puff himself up? Why is earth and ashes proud? Why does the proud rich man exalt himself above the poor man? Why does he despise the poor man? Why does he oppress the poor man? 576 Why does he either not give bread to the poor man out of stinginess, or take it away out of rapacity, and from him to whom he ought mercifully to give something of his own abundance, try cruelly to take away the little he has? He supposes that when he burdens the poor man he relieves himself; he thinks that when he afflicts the poor man he does himself some good. And he does not know that when he oppresses the poor man he lays a most heavy weight on himself, nor does he consider that whatever he plans concerning the poor man, he plans concerning himself. For he bestows good on himself when he does good to the poor man. But if he plans to do evil to the poor man, he will harm himself more than the poor man.

9. Let the rich man therefore do good to the poor man, and it will profit himself. Let him love mercy, and always bestow it on the poor man, so that he himself may find mercy in the day of tribulation (perhaps of retribution). Let him so consider himself placed above the poor man as to remember that he is set under God, the rich one. Let him not hesitate, then, to show the poor man the mercy which he delights to receive from God, the rich one. Let him remember that God is judge, who has eternal power over all things. For he sees the deeds of all; he will render to each according to his works (Matt. 16:27). Hence it is truly said that Judgement without mercy to him who has not shown mercy (James 2:13), and Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy (Matt. 5:7).

10. Let us therefore do judgement and justice, let us love mercy. And when we do judgement and justice and love mercy, we walk carefully with our God. He walks with God who advances in good conduct and works, who puts heavenly things before earthly, and eternal things before temporal. But each one must walk carefully: that is, he must not be high-minded, but fear; he must flee pride and attribute nothing good to his own merits, but in all that he has done well acknowledge the grace of God. This carefulness makes a person go with Christ along the way of humility and arrive at the height of the heavenly kingdom. Turning therefore to the Lord, let us together beseech his mercy, that he may grant us his grace, by which we may keep right judgement within ourselves, show justice to others, and, loving mercy, not oppress the poor but cherish them: so that in the sight of God, to whom we sing of mercy and judgement (Ps. 100:1), we may find mercy exalting itself above judgement.
